sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, M’Zab Valley
sources.note: Institutional description read in full indexed text. Uses the detailed synthesis dates 1012 to 1350, rather than the inconsistent tenth-century short description. Existing Algeria card uses this URL; runtime reuse included in budget.

sources.title: Augustin Jomier, Islam, réforme et colonisation: Une histoire de l’ibadisme en Algérie (1882 to 1962), publisher’s research summary (2020)
sources.note: Publisher’s substantial original research synopsis read, not the full book: French occupation of Mzab in 1882, independence in 1962, reformist scholarship and movement between Cairo, Tunis, Algiers and Mzab in the 1920s to 1950s.

sources.title: Boualem Remini, The Foggaras of the Oasis of Ghardaia (Algeria): The Sharing of Flood Waters, Larhyss Journal 36 (2018), 157 to 178
sources.note: Direct original PDF read. Its embedded title metadata incorrectly names an unrelated Madagascar article; printed title and content are the Ghardaia study. Field visits 2006 to 2018. Floodwater replenishes soil and shallow aquifer; no precise medieval construction date inferred from modern observation.

sources.title: Said Madani, An Ingenious Heritage System for Collecting and Distributing Flood Water in the M’zab Valley of Algeria, Blue Papers 1(2) (2022), 100 to 110
sources.note: Direct original PDF read, especially printed pages 102 and 104. Garden paths double as canals; opening widths depend on distance, plot area and palms. Controllers communicate by mirrors or fire. Does not repeat unqualified claims of unchanging society, perfect equality or universally unique invention.

sources.title: Sara Bekaddour, Nassim Ait-Mouheb and Tarik Hartani, Re-emergence of dry toilets and fecal nutrient reuse in M’zab cities, Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development 11(6) (2021), 983 to 993
sources.note: Full relevant original study read through indexed author ResearchGate text; direct publisher fetch failed. Interviews in 2019, 22 farmers, three former toilet cleaners and 15 association/civil-society participants. Historical chronology is interview-based, not excavated thirteenth-century toilets. No instructions for handling untreated waste or claim of proven health safety.

sources.title: Paul M. Love Jr, Catalog of Ibadi Manuscripts at the Special Collections Library of the Università degli Studi di Napoli L’Orientale (2017)
sources.note: Public PDF downloaded and read locally; web extractor rejected its 16 MB size. Printed page 5 rendered and visually checked. MS ARA 50, Kitab al-wada, folio 1b incipit begins الحمد لله. Catalogue dates copying to Rajab 1175 AH, identified as 1762 CE on page 19. This is a Libyan-provenance North African Ibadi example, not a Mzab manuscript.

sources.title: Paul M. Love Jr, Library Catalogs and Inventories, Ibadi Studies
sources.note: Direct author’s field-research page read: private household and larger libraries, inventories and codicological catalogues, family collections in Djerba and dispersed collections abroad. Wider Ibadi network explicitly distinguished from the imported Mzab polygon.

sources.title: Valentin Vydrin, Towards Proto-Mande, CNRS LLACAN conference abstract
sources.note: Indexed original research abstract read; direct PDF fetch failed. Mande family comprises 60 to 75 languages in Western and South-Eastern branches. Tentative glottochronological homeland and split estimates are not asserted as settled fact.

sources.title: Roderick J. McIntosh and Susan Keech McIntosh, Forgotten Tells of Mali, Expedition (1983)
sources.note: Direct original excavation-team account read. Uses observed settlement size, walls and imported materials, not its older abandonment date, proposed climate explanations or the hypothesis that every craft group occupied its own mound. Language identity of all excavated residents is not established.

sources.title: Roderick J. McIntosh and Susan Keech McIntosh, Initial perspectives on prehistoric subsistence in the Inland Niger Delta (Mali), World Archaeology 11(2) (1979)
sources.note: Original study abstract read in full indexed text: 1977 excavations found African rice and evidence of rice-fish-cattle subsistence. Avoids claiming that this older report alone establishes the first domestication date or ethnicity.

sources.title: Susan Keech McIntosh and Roderick J. McIntosh, Results of recent excavations at Jenné-jeno and Djenné, Mali
sources.note: Direct original author PDF read. Report for the 2001 Panafrican Congress, with bibliography updated through 2003. Pages 3 and 5 to 8: occupation through about 1400, limited wealth differentiation among surviving imports, and Djenné museum-site well in broadly fifteenth-to-seventeenth-century lower deposits. Site names and date scopes kept separate.

sources.title: Barbara E. Frank, Marks of Identity: Potters of the Folona (Mali) and Their “Mothers”, African Arts 40(1) (2007)
sources.note: Relevant full author article text and figure captions read through indexed author-hosted research copy. Printed page 37, figure 21: Fatoumata Kouyaté, Sissingué, 1992, shaping a pot by hand. Distinguishes local traditions and cross-community borrowing; no assertion that all Mande women used one method.

sources.title: Michael C. Carlos Museum, Hunter’s Shirt, Donson Dlokiw, object 1994.004.111
sources.note: Full indexed museum catalogue read; direct page returned 403. Malinke, Mali, late nineteenth to early twentieth century. Object materials and catalogue interpretation of added amulets are used as belief/practice, not supernatural efficacy.

sources.title: UNESCO, Cultural space of Sosso-Bala
sources.note: Full indexed institutional account read. Twenty slats, calabashes, Dökala family custody at Nyagassola, Balatigui teaching age seven upward. Ancient association is identified as tradition, not scientifically established instrument manufacture. Existing Guinea-card usage is included in combined URL budget.

sources.title: Michael Everson, Mamady Doumbouya, Baba Mamadi Diané and Karamo Kaba Jammeh, Proposal to add the N’Ko script to the BMP of the UCS, N2765 (8 June 2004)
sources.note: Direct original proposal read and printed page 4 visually rendered from downloaded PDF. The example tô is glossed name and shown in N’Ko. Modern Unicode transcription uses logical right-to-left letter order U+07D5 U+07D0 U+07EE. Does not adopt the proposal’s unverified medieval coronation story or speaker-count estimate.

sources.title: Unicode Standard 17.0, Chapter 19, section 19.4: N’Ko
sources.note: Section read in corresponding Unicode 16 text and checked against the existing cited version 17 source; same relevant wording. Script devised in 1949; marks for vowels and tone; decorative gbakurunen symbol represents three cooking stones. Same-work version reuse with the Guinea card is counted together.

proposedOverrides.name: Mande-speaking peoples
proposedOverrides.summary: Diverse Mande-speaking communities, regional towns, crafts, music and later writing.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Religious-regional label in the central Maghreb, not all Ibadis globally and not a revived Rustamid empire. Mzab is the main local focus. The detailed later water studies, colonial account and Libyan manuscript witness are explicitly dated and scoped. The polygon is not evidence that every enclosed resident followed one religion.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Two-word Arabic incipit faithfully transcribed by Paul Love, visually checked on printed catalogue page 5. The eighteenth-century Libyan book is explicitly a wider-network example; no fabricated thirteenth-century Mzab phrase.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: A broad cultural-language label, not Mali or Ghana under another name. The polygon extends far beyond defensible Mande language territory. Jenné-jeno examples are regional archaeological context, explicitly not proof that every resident spoke Mande. Later museum objects, fieldwork and N’Ko are dated. No current distribution back-projected as a medieval frontier.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: N2765 (2004), printed page 4 visually checked: tô, name, in N’Ko. Standard logical Unicode sequence U+07D5 U+07D0 U+07EE; avoid copying the Unicode website’s visually ordered text extraction without its bidi styling. Script creation 1949, not medieval. Gbakurunen U+07F7 meaning verified separately in the standard.
